newsitem.title: USA: Mir difficulties concern U.S. space agency.
newsitem.headline: Mir difficulties concern U.S. space agency.

text.p: The failure of a crucial pair of oxygen generators on Russia's Mir space station limited air supply for the two Russians and one American aboard and was worrying, NASA officials said on Friday.
"You hate to see your margins reduced in any area." Frank Culbertson, who head's NASA's shuttle-Mir programme, said. "Its not a comfortable situation to be in, but that's where they are right now."

The failure of the so-called Elektron devices, which generate breathing oxygen from waste water, has forced the crew to use a back-up chemical system identical to one that sparked a fire on the station two weeks ago.

"They have assured me that they are very comfortable with doing this," Culbertson told Reuters. "They really don't have much choice right now because they have to make sure they maintain a certain level of oxygen."

Russian officials estimated the chemical system would provide enough oxygen for two months, by which time fresh supplies and spare parts for the bulky equipment should be delivered to the station by an unmanned resupply rocket.

The failure of the twin Elektron systems, and the fire on Feb. 22, which destroyed a chemical generator, means the crew of three will have to rely on the sole remaining chemical system for their oxygen supply.

If that chemical system should fail, there is about five day's worth of emergency oxygen in cylinders aboard Mir, but after that the crew would be forced to leave the station in a Soyuz return capsule.
"If you have no further means of producing oxygen, you have no choice," Culbertson, a veteran astronaut, said. "I don't think it would be an abandon ship deal; it would be an orderly departure."

NASA officials were following developments aboard Mir closely. U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger is nearing the half way point of a four-month stay on Mir. His Russian crewmates, Vasily Tsibliev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin are 23 days into a 197-day mission.
"I think that this was certainly the worst situation they've had; a fire followed by mechanical problems that add up to a marginal situation for them," Culbertson said.
"I don't know for sure that they would categorize this as the worst, but I think it's something they are working pretty hard to get through and are being pretty realistic about."

The station's chemical oxygen generators raised additional concerns following last month's brief fire. A crack in a lithium perchlorate canister used by the devices was blamed for the blaze which filled the complex with choking smoke and caused some minor damage.
There are about 185 lithium perchlorate canisters left on the station and over a hundred are thought to be safe for use. One or two will be used each day.

The U.S. shuttle Atlantis was to return to the station in mid-May to pick up Linenger and drop off a replacement. Culbertson said it was unlikely that the shuttle launch could be brought forward to help with repairs work.

Friday's problem was the latest to hit the cash-strapped Russian space programme, which has been struggling to fulfil its obligations to provide a crucial command module for the planned NASA-led international space station.
Culbertson said the latest technical trouble aboard Mir should not reflect badly on the Russian's space capabilities.
"The Mir had a service-life of five years when they launched it and they're in their 12th year already, so I think it actually demonstrates that they build a pretty robust system," he said.
